title: Low-friction tool integration spec + lazy-parse stream (PRD draft)
content:
Purpose: quick PRD draft describing a new streaming framing + tool-calling surface designed to reduce client integration friction and allow optional 'lazy' parsing on the client side. This is meant as a developer-friendly evolution of current streaming (SSE/CHUNKED) with first-class tool events and typed-output hints while keeping backwards compatibility.

Context and motivation:
- Engineers keep tripping over two pain points: (1) integrating tool calls requires fragile, out-of-band message parsing and (2) clients are forced to eagerly parse every JSON token, which increases CPU/latency on low-power clients (mobile, edge).
- We want a single stream that: (a) cleanly represents tool lifecycle events, (b) provides lightweight framing for structured outputs, (c) supports a lazy-parse mode where clients can skip parsing ephemeral token text until needed.

Goals (what success looks like):
- SDKs can support tool integrations with <10 lines of glue for common languages.
- No increase in median p99 latency for hosted streaming responses (target: +<=5ms).
- Clients can opt into lazy-parse mode and reduce client-side CPU by 20–60% for long-running generation sessions.
- Backwards compatible: existing streaming clients continue to work without changes.

Non-goals:
- Not trying to replace function-calling semantics; this is primarily about the on-the-wire representation and SDK ergonomics.
- Not solving complex distributed tool orchestration (that's a later phase).

Proposed surface (high-level):
1) Framed stream with minimal envelope: each chunk is prefixed with a one-byte type marker and length (length optional for SSE clients). Markers: T (text/token), E (event/control), R (tool-result), S (structured-metadata), C (checksum/close).
   - Example raw (conceptual): "T:...
E:tool-invoke:{id}
T:...
R:{id}:stdout:...
R:{id}:result:{json}
C:done"
2) Tool calling: tool lifecycle events are explicit event frames (E) with stable fields: event-type, tool-id, call-id, status. Tool result frames use R with an attached MIME-type hint (application/json, text/plain, ndjson).
3) Typed/structured hints: S frames carry a compact schema hint id and canonical JSON-paths for where typed objects will appear in subsequent tokens. These are optional and small (aim <120 bytes).
4) Lazy-parse mode: client opts-in via header X-Redwood-Lazy-Parse: 1. In this mode, T frames may be emitted as either full-text or as token-refs (short binary indices) that allow client to request expansion on demand (TODO: mechanism sketched below).

Why this helps:
- Clear separation: tool control vs user-facing token text improves client logic and reduces accidental parsing errors.
- Lazy-parse lets mobile/edge clients do cheap pass-through until they need to materialize a structured object (e.g., display, call tool).
- SDK wrappers can expose a small state machine and typed events instead of raw stream parsing code.

SDK ergonomics (developer-facing):
- Provide first-class stream parser libraries for Node, Python, and a small runtime in Go and Rust. API shape (Node sketch):
  const stream = client.stream({model, prompt, lazyParse: true})
  stream.on('token', t => /* tokens as strings OR token-metadata refs */)
  stream.on('tool.invoke', meta => /* decide to allow/deny, attach args */)
  stream.on('tool.stdout', (id, chunk) => /* incremental stdout */)
  stream.on('tool.result', (id, typedPayload) => /* typed result object OR opaque blob */)
  stream.on('structuredHint', hint => /* schema hint: validate locally or wait */)
  await stream.closed()
- Backpressure: SDK exposes pause()/resume() hooks mapped to underlying TCP/HTTP2 flow control where available. For SSE/HTTP-streaming we add an advisory window header so servers can avoid unbounded buffering for slow clients.
- Parsers should default to eager-string conversion for compatibility; lazy parsing must be opt-in at stream creation.

Server-side considerations:
- Emitting S frames requires computing lightweight schema hints from model output predictions; heuristics will be added to detect likely JSON blobs and emit hints proactively.
- We must ensure that tool-result frames are atomic and signed (optional checksum C frame) for client verification.
- Fallback: when client doesn't support framing, server emits plain tokens (existing format).

Wire compatibility strategy:
- Header negotiation: Client includes Accept-Framing: framed-v2 (or none). If server supports framed-v2, it switches to framed mode. Otherwise stream stays legacy.
- Lazy-parse header X-Redwood-Lazy-Parse triggers token-ref workflow otherwise server uses full-text tokens.

Telemetry and observability:
- Emit token/event-level IDs so traces can be correlated across model, tool-exec, and telemetry logs. Tag tool events with cost buckets.
- Sampled payload capture: for privacy we only capture schema-hint metadata and token counts in logs; full payloads captured only in controlled debug sessions.

Migration path and rollout plan (milestones):
- M1 (2 weeks): prototype stream parser + small server-side emitter for a single model (canary) — internal only.
- M2 (4–6 weeks): SDK wrappers (Node + Py) with opt-in framed-v2 + lazy-parse. Run pilot with 3 internal integrations (Search, Console assistant).
- M3 (8–12 weeks): scale tooling (tool-result signing, checksum, telemetry), docs, and public-facing opt-in.
- M4 (post-launch): gather metrics, determine whether to make framed-v2 default for new clients.

Open questions / Risks:
- Token-ref expansion API complexity: Do we support a pull-back mechanism (client says please expand ref id) or do we embed expansion hints inside R frames?
- Interoperability with existing SDKs that assume simple SSE: need adapters that emulate legacy events.
- Mobile/edge offline scenarios: lazy-parse reduces CPU but increases bursty network behavior when expansions requested. Need heuristics to prefetch.
- Security: tool results may contain sensitive structured data. Policy controls needed (masking, redaction).

Implementation TODOs (short actionable items):
- [ ] Create binary framing RFC doc with exact byte layout (serving-runtime owning).
- [ ] Implement header negotiation and simple framed-v2 emitter in staging. (infra + serving-runtime)
- [ ] Prototype Node/Python stream parser + example app for tools team. (developer-experience)
- [ ] Telemetry schema changes for event ids and sample flags. (observability)
- [ ] Security review for tool-result signing and data retention. (security-and-compliance)

Stakeholders and owners:
- Product: Sofia Patel (owner), Jin Park (PM)
- Engineering: Serving runtime (TBD), SDK x-ing (Liam O'Connor), infra (Diego Ramos)
- DevEx: Amaya Chen (sdk examples + docs)
- Security & Compliance: reviewer assigned during M2

Notes to self / rough ideas:
- Could we piggyback on http2 stream ids for easier client-side expansion? probably makes sense for long-lived connections.
- Small optimization: when schema-hint S references a JMESPath-like pointer, client can pre-allocate object shapes and validate incrementally.
- Keep tooling simple: initial V1 should focus on tool lifecycle events + typed result frames; lazy token-ref expansion can be V1 alpha with opt-in for internal customers.

References and inspiration:
- previous streaming playbooks in this folder (see linked artifacts)
- SSE vs HTTP/2 streaming patterns notes from infra

Accepting feedback: I expect design options to be debated — particularly the token-ref mechanism and whether framing should be binary vs text. Please leave comments inline or ping on #prod-hosted-api.

Quick status: draft, needs serving-runtime feasibility check (byte framing), and SDK prototype to validate ergonomics.
